title: Getting started and finding your way around

sections.title: 1.1 Choose how to launch StarOrbit
sections.html:
Edition How to start Resources
Web Open StarOrbit online and wait for the model. The site loads models, textures and music as needed.
Portable Download the ZIP from Releases, extract the entire folder and open StarOrbit.html. The basic spacecraft, orbits, Earth and sky work offline. Previously cached extensions are available at the original browser address.
Local service On macOS, use the bundled app if included, or launch the command file. With Python 3 you can also run python3 scripts/serve.py --open from the extracted folder. The viewer runs in the browser. The service can convert supported cloud data and retrieve solar images.

The website, local service and directly opened HTML keep separate settings and libraries. Export the scene before changing editions. Keep weather snapshots and custom spacecraft files for use in the other edition. See photography and sharing and offline data.

Open StarOrbit Pro from the header or StarOrbitPro.html. Configure a LEO satellite and two 24-hour plans to compare battery energy and board temperature. Load the station example or your own OEM under Orbit source and reference. Propagate from its initial state or drive both plans with the supplied orbit. Select an excursion or the largest orbit deviation to inspect that instant in 3D. Export mission and result JSON, orbital OEM and engineering CSV from Mission files.

Choose Load lake observation example, then run 24 hours. Compare raw downlink and onboard filtering by useful images delivered, latency, battery reserve and board temperature. Select an image and an exposure, processing or downlink time to see it in 3D, or read why delivery was incomplete. The example uses editable hardware assumptions and repeatable simulated image labels. Export the image ledger as CSV.

sections.title: 1.2 Explore the station on your first visit
sections.html:
Ask an operating question or open the spacecraft key diagram from Help. In the main view, dragging the middle button up or down also zooms.

Open sections in the left sidebar to find mission, time, assembly and environment settings. Open “? Help” at the top right; on smaller screens open “Tools” first. Switch between the guided tour and the manual, browse the contents or resume where you left off. If the scene is very dark, the station may be over the ocean at night. Wait for daylight or move the orbit timeline to a gold sunlit segment.

To do this Try this
Inspect the model Left-drag to orbit, right-drag to pan, and scroll to zoom. On a touchscreen, drag with one finger to orbit; use two fingers to pan or zoom.
Find the spacecraft again Double-click its model, or choose a camera target and “Recenter” in the view menu. “Fit all” frames all spacecraft.
Switch between a close view and the orbit In “Orbit & time” choose “Follow spacecraft” or “Orbit overview”. The view menu also offers top, bottom, side, oblique and horizon views.
Hide module labels Clear “Spacecraft labels” under “Display & views”. You can also show the orbit, Sun direction or fill light.
Compose a clean picture “Photography & scenes” → “Photo mode” hides the interface and the minimap. Press Esc to return. See Chapter 10.

sections.title: 1.3 Position windows and direct keyboard input
sections.html:
Activate Resize window in the title area. Drag either side to change width or drag a corner to resize both axes. Arrow keys and compact/expanded presets are available. Esc finishes. Narrow and wide layouts remember their own sizes.

“Xuntian viewfinder” and “Orbit map” are independent windows. Leave both open, drag their title bars to reposition them, or stack them on a small screen. The browser remembers the layout. In “Display & views” → “Window layout” you can lock window positions or restore the original arrangement. The camera target determines what you see. The navball and free-flight controls have a separate choice of vehicle. Click the navball, optical view or training display before using its keys. In the viewfinder the steering keys aim the telescope; on the navball they rotate the selected vehicle.

sections.title: 2.1 Switch missions and check the orbit
sections.html: In “Mission selection” → “Current mission” choose the station, Dongfanghong 1 or an imported vehicle. The simulation time, Earth, clouds, sky and graphics follow you between missions. Each mission has its own orbit, orientation, rotation and camera. Returning to the station restores its assembly and array angles. The station supports assembly, solar arrays, the Xuntian telescope and crew or cargo flights. Dongfanghong 1 can point along its trajectory or hold an inertial axis. Its nominal spin is 120 rotations per minute of simulation time; use 1× to watch it. The music note offers the historical recording and simulated telemetry. See Chapter 10. For dates before 2000 (UTC+8), Dongfanghong 1 uses a historical reconstruction based mainly on records from 25 April to 2 May 1970. From 2000 onward it uses the modern orbit. Check the source, epoch, coverage and computation mode under “Orbit data”. “Go to valid interval” returns to the covered interval. A custom mission with only a model can be inspected; add matching orbit data to obtain orbital readouts.

sections.title: 2.2 Import a spacecraft model
sections.html:
1. Open “Mission selection” and choose “Download configuration template”. Give the mission a unique ID, name and category. Set the model filename and prepare a GLB 2.0 file with its meshes and textures embedded.
  2. Set metresPerUnit to metres per model unit (1 for metres, 0.001 for millimetres). Choose perpendicular forward and normal axes using signed X, Y or Z for forwardAxis and normalAxis.
  3. Set orbit.file to the matching filename if supplied; a model-only mission can use a null orbit. GP/OMM records must match the spacecraft. In “Import spacecraft” select the configuration JSON, GLB and specified orbit file together. Choose the imported mission in “Current mission”. The configuration, GLB and orbit files have limits of 1, 128 and 30 MB respectively (decimal). Keep the source files for another browser. See orbit import.

sections.title: 2.3 Set a date, pause and step through time
sections.html:
The main window shows UTC+8 (Beijing time). Under “Orbit & time” choose “Custom time”, enter year through seconds and press “Go to time” to pause at that instant. Left/right arrows select a field; up/down arrows change its value. The 12-hour/24-hour switch changes only the display. “Live now” follows the current time again.

Purpose Action
Pause or resume Use “Pause” or “Resume”. To catch up to real time choose “Live now”.
Compare nearby positions Choose 1s, 1m, 10m, 1h or 1d, then use the signed step buttons. For example, choose 10m and +10m. Playback keeps its current state. One day is 24 hours.
Accelerate “Playback speed” offers 1×, 10×, 60×, 300× and 1000×. Playback starts from the current simulated instant.
Explore outside the recorded interval Jump or step to the date. The viewer continues the orbit from the nearest endpoint and accounts for effects including orbital-plane precession. Check the computation mode beside the readout.

sections.title: 2.4 Read the map and the orbit event timeline
sections.html: On the orbit map, cyan marks the past track and gold the future track. Light and dark areas of the map mark day and night on the ground. The spacecraft data panel reports its own illumination, altitude and speed. Click a track or drag the position marker to select a time. While playing, the map retains the playback rate. While paused, it stays paused. Focus the map and press a left or right arrow to step one minute and pause. Under “Orbit & time” → “Orbital event timeline” enable “Show timeline” and select 3, 12 or 24 hours. Here gold indicates sunlight at the spacecraft, dark blue indicates full shadow and the transition indicates partial shadow. Filter eclipse transitions, apsides or equator crossings. Drag to a time, select an event or step between events. Start 30 seconds before an event or enable “Pause at events” to watch the transition.

sections.title: 3.1 Choose a station configuration
sections.html:
Geographic and Xuntian finder labels default on. Opening the finder frames the telescope in the main view, with an 8× exterior field guide by default.

Choose the station mission and open “Module assembly”. Selecting a preset replaces the current assembly. To keep a custom configuration, export a scene first under “Photography & scenes” → “Scene sharing”.

Preset Contents
“Tianhe only” The root Tianhe core, with five available ports.
“Three modules” Tianhe, Wentian and Mengtian. The forward, lower and aft ports are available for spacecraft or additional cores.
“Full assembly” All three modules, two Shenzhou spacecraft on the forward and lower node ports, and one Tianzhou at the aft port. Xuntian flies alongside as a separate vehicle.

sections.title: 3.2 Extend the station and remove a branch
sections.html:
1. Begin with “Three modules”. At Tianhe’s “Node forward” choose “Tianhe core”. The sidebar now lists two numbered Tianhe cores.
  2. On Tianhe 2 choose another core at its forward port to add a third, or choose a different port to make a branch. Each new core connects by its aft port and exposes four node ports. Its panel identifies the parent core and the connecting port.
  3. To restore the three original modules, set the forward port on Tianhe 1 to “Empty”. Tianhe 2 and its descendants are removed together; Wentian and Mengtian remain. To remove only Tianhe 3, change the port on Tianhe 2 instead. Replacing a core also removes its children. If a spacecraft occupied the port earlier, select it again to reinstall it.
  4. Select a preset to replace the assembly. “Reset assembly” also restores the corresponding array angles and view. Ordinary scene files can store up to 256 assembly instances. “Free-flying Xuntian” shows Xuntian as a separate companion. You can repeat module types. Rotate a large assembly to inspect the connections and the clearance around its solar arrays.

sections.title: 3.3 Adjust the arrays and read their illumination
sections.html: In “Solar arrays” choose the module instance. Core number and port distinguish duplicates. Move the sliders for assembly rotation or panel angle. Link the left and right arrays or adjust them separately; Wentian and Mengtian can also move together. Use the spin demonstration to see an axis, and “Reset angles” to clear the manual angle. Manual adjustment exits automatic Sun tracking; re-enable “Sun tracking” to resume. Enable “Account for body/array occlusion” to include shadows from structures and other arrays. The effective sunlit fraction combines front-face orientation, clear panel area and the visible fraction of the Sun, weighted by panel area. In eclipse it can be zero even while tracking. Pause in a sunlit part of the timeline to compare angles. Electrical output would also depend on factors such as cell efficiency.

sections.title: 3.4 Take control with the main navball
sections.html:
Open the control diagram from the navball. Keys light up when the flight controls have keyboard focus.

In “Spacecraft attitude” set roll X, pitch Y and yaw Z with sliders or numerical entries (±180°, 0.1° increments). “Reset attitude” clears these offsets. The mission determines the reference attitude. Changing an offset keeps the time and orbit. Enable “Show navball”, check the selected vehicle, and click the ball to take keyboard control. The first input starts a 1× near-orbit exercise.

Control Action
W/S, A/D, Q/E Pitch down/up, yaw left/right, roll left/right.
H/N, J/L, I/K With RCS enabled, translate forward/back, left/right, down/up. Releasing the key leaves the existing velocity.
R, T, F, Caps Lock R toggles RCS, T toggles SAS attitude hold, F temporarily reverses SAS while held. Caps Lock selects 20% fine control.
Brake or return With RCS enabled, hold “Relative brake” to reduce relative velocity. “Pause flight” freezes the exercise. “Restore observation” restores the reference position and attitude. Esc or a click outside releases the keyboard.

On the main page SAS starts on and RCS off. SAS damps rotation; use reverse thrust or relative braking for translation. The full navball adds angular rate, relative speed and position offset. Select prograde, retrograde, radial, normal or target directions for automatic pointing; manual input takes over. A dashed marker indicates the far side. This exercise covers the vicinity within 10 km of the reference orbit. Changing mission, time, playback rate or starting free flight ends it.

sections.title: 3.5 Depart, dock and resume a saved flight
sections.html:
1. Choose a docked ship in Free flight and enter the cockpit, or use Pilot beside its port. The flight copies the current assembly, wing angles and orbit. Choose Undock to start flying. Ships share the mission clock. Above RCS thrust settings, find the controls and the toggle for the live docking camera window, initially on.
  2. Use the rotation and translation keys above. In free flight RCS starts on. Hold “Relative brake” in the on-screen controls to reduce drift. The exterior camera shows the formation, the navball shows attitude and velocity, and the docking camera looks down your port axis. Green marks velocity; the purple diamond points to the original port.
  3. Watch port range, closing speed, sideways offset and attitude. Positive closing speed means an approach. Correct drift and match the port angles before moving in slowly. Use “Docking assist” from a suitable position. After a collision use “Restore checkpoint” to try again.
  4. RCS settings affect the selected ship. Docking tolerances apply to all ships in this flight; the default contact-speed tolerance is 0.20 m/s. Refer to the instrument panel for angular rate, position and speed checks.
  5. “Save flight” or “Back to observation” saves the flight. On the same browser and address open free flight and choose “Resume selected flight”. A restored flight starts paused. The free-flight save is separate from a normal scene file.

sections.title: 3.6 Practice rendezvous and docking in the lab
sections.html:
Open “Mission lab” → “Rendezvous & docking”. The four starting cases are final alignment (about 12 m), standard approach (200 m), recovery from offset and drift (50 m), and random position (50–500 m ahead). To practice the final metres, choose final alignment, keep beginner assistance on, select assisted approach and press start/continue.

  • Approach and release. Training runs at 1×, 2× or 5×. Standard approach has 30 m and 5 m hold points; final alignment uses the 5 m point. Hold the position, speed, attitude and offsets within limits for two seconds, then press GO. Station keeping counteracts drift. Use retreat to move outward or pause training to stop the clock.
  • Manual control. Click the training display or hold the on-screen controls. Manual input takes over from assisted approach. Disabling beginner assistance also disables hold points, the corridor, automatic stabilization and relative braking. Use reverse thrust to cancel drift.
  • Instruments. Compare the sight with lateral offset, axial closing speed, alignment and angular rate. The gold dashed line predicts 60 seconds without further thrust; blue shows the flown track. The docking-speed limit defaults to 0.15 m/s and applies to total relative speed at contact.
  • Review. Open “Replay & report” for contact readings, release events and violations. Export JSON for the full record or CSV for a spreadsheet. Starting another run replaces the current record; save it first if needed.

sections.title: 4.1 Open the viewfinder and compare the two views
sections.html: In the Chinese station mission open “Xuntian viewfinder” on the toolbar, or “Open Xuntian viewfinder” under “Module assembly”. On small screens open “Tools” first. The main camera moves near Xuntian, while the inset shows what its optics see. Drag the star field and watch the tube turn outside. Use “Frame both craft” to frame the formation or “Exterior: telescope close-up” for a closer exterior view.

sections.title: 4.2 View Vega and Beijing at the same instant
sections.html:
On page 6 of the short tour choose “View Vega” or “View Beijing”. Both use the same paused example. Switch between them, then choose “Return to my scene” to return. To prepare the observation manually:

  1. Use the bundled station orbit. In “Orbit & time” select custom time, enter 2026-11-05 13:44:00 (UTC+8) and choose “Go to time”. The simulation pauses.
  2. Open “Xuntian viewfinder”. If you moved the telescope, choose “Restore initial position”. Type Vega in “Find a celestial object or city” and click the matching result or press Enter. Use the wheel, two fingers or the equivalent focal-length slider to frame the star.
  3. Search the same field for Beijing and choose the city result. Watch the tube turn towards Earth. Read “At the crosshair” for the geographic position and choose “Capture PNG” to save the composition. Both targets are clear of the Earth at this instant; Beijing is in daylight. Cloud cover affects visible surface detail.
  4. Search for Vega again to point back at it. When available, “Return to star field” restores the previous sky field and field of view. “Live now” on the main page restores real time.

sections.title: 4.3 Search, track and release a target
sections.html:
Right-click a position or long-press on touch to inspect it. Read its description, centre without changing zoom, track a supported target or plan an image of the field. Coordinates are available for unmatched positions.

Search by star name, constellation abbreviation, HIP number, Messier or NGC number, nebula, Chinese asterism or member star, planet, Moon or city. Try Vega, M31, NGC 7000, Mars or Beijing. Cities rotate with Earth; a city may be behind the planet at another time. The Moon and Mars have dedicated observation cards. For a Solar System target, “View in main scene” points the main camera in the same direction.

Goal Action
Follow a target Choose it from the search results. A city follows its location on Earth; a sky target follows its direction.
Hold the current center Choose “Pin this sightline”. On Earth it follows the ground position, in the sky it holds the celestial direction, and on the station it follows the selected point on a part. Steering while pinned updates the anchor.
Let the stars drift Choose “Move with the orbit”. The initial composition is retained and the telescope then turns with the orbit. Pausing the simulation also stops the drift.
Find image detail Zoom in and inspect “Sky imagery” and “Image sources and bands”. Catalog entries supply positions; the selected survey supplies imagery where it has coverage.

sections.title: 4.4 Look at the ground, the station and the formation
sections.html: “Look at the ground” points to the sub-satellite point. Expand “Station, Earth and formation” for the station, horizon, nadir and sunlit-surface presets. Drag the formation diagram to move along or across the orbit and use the height slider for radial displacement. A clearance zone surrounds the station and arrays. “Restore initial position” returns Xuntian to about 52 m ahead of the station, looking along the flight direction with space at the top of the frame. “Show telescope field in exterior view” draws the optical cone on the exterior view. Scale its exterior depiction from 0.25× to 8×; equivalent focal length determines the photo field. Check the vehicle on the navball before flying Xuntian. Dragging, searching or pinning in the viewfinder returns control to its optics.

sections.title: 4.5 Frame an image and read the crosshair
sections.html:
Widening the window enlarges the actual optical image. In a wide finder, search and capture stay on the left and settings scroll on the right. Hide settings gives the sky more room. Open Aiming marker to change its shape, color or size, hide it, or apply the style to every aiming marker.

Open the coordinate explanation for the current J2000 reading. RA uses hours, minutes and seconds. One hour equals 15°. Positive and negative declination indicate north and south of the celestial equator.

Control Effect
Equivalent focal length A longer setting magnifies a smaller field. Use the wheel or pinch gesture as well. A visible planet can grow from a point into a disk.
Aperture A larger effective aperture reveals fainter stars. A higher limiting-magnitude number means fainter stars can appear.
Exposure compensation Changes brightness without changing the aim.
Image rotation Adjust the slider or focus the viewfinder and use Q/E to roll the frame. The reset arrow restores zero roll. W/S tilt down/up and A/D steer left/right; drag or use the arrow keys as well.
Enlarged view “Enlarge view” redraws the same composition in a larger window. The readout gives display dimensions and loaded Earth/sky tiers. Choose the photo size separately.

The crosshair identifies the current center independently of the tracked target. Angular offset is the angular separation from the target center. For a Solar System body, distance is measured from the telescope to its center. Reliable stellar parallax gives an estimate in light-years from the Sun. For station parts or terrain the readout gives line-of-sight range. Ground positions also show coordinates and distance to the nearest listed city center. An empty sky field shows celestial coordinates.

sections.title: 4.6 Labels, imagery and photographs
sections.html: “Finder sky annotations” controls the preview. “Include annotations in photos” controls the exported PNG. Both share categories, sky tradition and density from the main sky-chart settings. To aim using names but save a clean picture, enable the first switch only. The finder saves its own image source and uses it for its photos; see Chapter 6 for optical surveys and Webb fields. Select 1440×900, 2560×1600 or 3840×2400 and press “Capture PNG”. Check the displayed source while detail loads. “Suggested field” offers other sky fields. For a full orbit of exposures open the survey plan in the mission lab. On a live retake choose the tile, center it, record it and open the four-tile result. See the survey plan.

sections.title: 4.7 Observe the Sun
sections.html:
Use Return to previous view or press Esc in the solar finder. Manually pan the whole solar disk out of view to continue looking at the new sky direction. A return control takes you back to the Sun.

In the viewfinder choose “Solar observing”, or open its card in “Data & resources” and choose “Observe the Sun in Xuntian”. Pick a band to match the structure of interest.

Band Look for
HMI white light Photosphere and sunspots
AIA 171 Å Coronal loops
AIA 304 Å Prominences and the transition region
AIA 131 Å Hot active regions, when present in the observation

SDO images have their own UTC observation time. AIA uses false color. The simulation time determines the viewing geometry while the loaded observation supplies the solar texture. Choose 2K (default) or 1K. Changing bands in the viewfinder preserves the composition; “Frame the Sun” recenters the disk. On the local service, “Update image” checks the selected band. The web viewer can import a solar snapshot exported by the desktop version. Adjust exposure, zoom or roll, then choose “Capture PNG” to save the image with its source and both times. Use “Optical view” for normal optical rendering or “Return to star field” for the previous sky field.

title: Earth, cities and the Solar System

sections.title: 5.1 Travel from orbit to a place on Earth
sections.html:
1. In the left sidebar open “Orbit & time”. Choose “Ground observation” below the view selector.
  2. Type a place name and choose a local catalog result. Press Enter or use the search button for online place-name matching. For coordinates, expand “Coordinates & map”, enter latitude and longitude, then choose “Go here”. You can also pick a point on the map.
  3. Drag to look around and use the wheel to change the field of view. “Save location” adds the location to your places. The map at the right shows your heading and nearby place names. Its title collapses the map, and the plus/minus buttons change its scale.
  4. The top bar switches between ground observation, the Solar System and interstellar travel. “Return to orbit” returns to the spacecraft. This browser remembers your last ground location, heading, field of view and speed setting.

In the 8K orbit overview, zoom in on a place and select “Descend here”. Return to orbit to restore that view. The overview, ground observer and Xuntian share terrain imagery. In Data and resources, switch between cards and a list, then tick or drag across items to delete them together.

Stargazing. While exploring the ground, choose “Set up telescope here” to track the sky in a side window. Stargazing opens the expanded view directly. Expand or collapse the view and zoom continuously with a wheel or pinch. Looking around the main scene preserves tracking. The left panel offers field of view, aperture, exposure, survey imagery, labels, offline fields and eyepiece photos. Finder enhancement, daytime terrain and a height of 50 m above ground start enabled. Use the roaming location or an independent site. Pan and zoom the large map and confirm a position. Put the telescope away to return to roaming.

Drag sideways in the main view to turn with the horizon level. Drag vertically to look up or down. An upward drag stops at the zenith (90°). Release and drag up again to look beyond it. With frame rotation at zero, dragging sideways in the eyepiece keeps elevation constant and the horizon level. Filter stars by magnitude. Satellite labels include density, minimum elevation, broadband constellations and catalogue filters. Calibrated satellites show an estimated magnitude.

sections.title: 5.2 Move, change altitude and view city lights
sections.html:
Click the scene to use the keyboard. H/N move forward/back, J/L left/right, I/K down/up. W/S tilt down/up, A/D turn and Space stops movement. Your speed depends on altitude and the speed setting. Enter metres in the altitude field for a precise height.

Button Height What to look for
“Return to ground” Near the local terrain Mountains, horizon and the local sky
“High altitude” About 10 km City layout, roads and patches of night lighting
“Low Earth orbit” About 400 km Coastlines, curvature and cloud bands
“Whole Earth” About 20,000 km The globe and the day/night boundary

The default 2025 night-light map has a resolution of about 500 m. Close to the ground, light from neighboring city blocks merges. Choose “High altitude” to see the overall pattern. Daytime city imagery uses a separate source; places including Beijing and Seattle have finer surface detail.

sections.title: 5.3 Manage city imagery, terrain and the cache
sections.html: In “Data & resources” open the city imagery collection, search for a city and view it or download the complete offline package. Bundled 10 m daytime imagery covers about 40×40 km in Beijing and 20×20 km in Seattle. Imagery supplies the surface colors and elevation supplies the relief. Under “Earth and terrain” → “Surface streaming and cache” control on-demand satellite imagery. Default radii are 120 km for imagery and 160 km for elevation; each can be set to 20–400 km. Movement and altitude changes update the covered area. The main globe and Xuntian can reuse these resources. Clearing roaming imagery removes automatic downloads but retains complete offline city packages. Elevation has its own cache. Move to another area or use the button to continue loading the current view. Stored data belongs to this browser and address.

sections.title: 5.4 Observe and photograph the sky from the ground
sections.html:
Right-click the ground sky or eyepiece, long-press on touch, or use the object actions button. The sky locator shows the local star pattern, field on the celestial sphere and local horizon. The separate eyepiece reports its own direction.

Ground exploration, the finder and the telescope eyepiece default to chart labels and up to a 16K Milky Way. The planetary observatory now offers sky cultures, labels and imagery sources.

Enter a date and time in UTC+8 and choose “Go to time”, or use “Now” for the present. Pause or advance by a minute, an hour or a day per second. Reverse playback is available at an hour per second. Ground and Solar System views share the selected time. Under “Sky & annotations” select the natural sky for local daylight and darkness. The enhanced Milky Way and DSS survey settings show stellar imagery. Use “See the sky through terrain” to locate a constellation behind a mountain. “Take photo” saves the current sky, location and time, including your labels and terrain visibility. See sky-chart controls.

sections.title: 5.5 Explore the Earth–Moon system and planetary moons
sections.html:
1. Choose “Solar System” and the Earth–Moon, inner Solar System or full Solar System scale. Select an observation target to follow it; drag to orbit and scroll to zoom. Toggle the orbit lines as needed.
  2. Use the enlarged-body display to pick out small bodies in wide views. Turn it off for physical radii. Both modes use the same positions and orbital distances.
  3. In the planetary satellite systems choose Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Neptune and select a satellite. Read its radius, period and distance from the planet’s center. The Moon and the four Galilean moons use astronomical calculations. The other 15 listed major satellites use ephemerides for 2026–2030; follow the displayed date range.
  4. For Earth, the Moon, Mars or the Sun, open the observation window for more detail. Return to your observing site for the ground view, or use “Return to orbit” for the spacecraft.

title: Sky surveys, star charts and interstellar travel

sections.title: 6.1 Compare telescope images of the same sky field
sections.html:
The main view and finder remember their own image source and artwork background. Photos use the finder selection. Selecting DSS or Pan-STARRS shows the survey at wide angles and loads more detail as you zoom. Hubble and Webb use the published image colours.

Source What you see
Automatic Loads available detail as you magnify the field.
Original Milky Way The original background for wide-field views.
DSS optical or Pan-STARRS optical Compare two optical surveys of the same region. Allow detail to load. Uncached regions require a connection.
Webb IR (JWST) Expand “Image sources and bands” and choose “View Cosmic Cliffs”, or search the viewfinder for Cosmic Cliffs. This bundled color composite uses Webb infrared observations.

Hubble and Webb accept a Milky Way, DSS, Pan-STARRS or blank background. Choose Blank to see only registered image footprints. Use the image catalogue to point at a work.

Automatic mode uses the Milky Way at wide angles. With an explicit optical survey, missing tiles and uncovered areas are black. Uncached data requires a connection. Check the sources panel for the actual credits and observing date, or manage saved fields under Data and resources.

Choose Hubble Telescope and select a background. In Browse sky images, filter by Hubble gallery and search M31, M51 or the Pillars of Creation. Open a work for its preview, instrument, bands and credits. Point the main sky or Xuntian at a registered image. Switching the source preserves pointing and focal length.

Open a card to read about the scene, the object and how the image was made. Registered images show the field centre. Object entries show their catalogue position. Both use J2000 right ascension and declination. Browsing keeps your current view.

sections.title: 6.2 Compare the Big Dipper and Ursa Major
sections.html:
The star chart defaults to the equatorial grid, ecliptic, full deep-sky catalog and 0.95 label density.

  1. Open “Geography & star chart” → “Sky annotations” and enable “Show sky annotations in main view”. Choose “Traditional Chinese asterisms” under the sky-culture selector.
  2. In “Explore Chinese asterisms” choose the Purple Forbidden Enclosure and the Big Dipper. Identify the ladle in the member chart, then select “Locate in main view”. In the station mission, “Locate in Xuntian” aims the telescope instead. With the bundled orbit, all seven stars clear the Earth at 2026-11-05 13:44 UTC+8, the same time as the Xuntian example.
  3. Enable the asterism lines and artwork. Keep the camera fixed and switch to the Western constellations. Compare the stars with the lines, name and artwork of Ursa Major. The Chinese index covers 32 regions: the three enclosures, 28 lunar mansions and southern additions. Choose all regions to browse every entry. Certain regions have overview illustrations for a celestial symbol or enclosure. Single-asterism artwork, its brightness, overview artwork and overview opacity have separate controls. Member-chart numbers identify the stars in that chart. The Western chart has 88 constellations, with separate names, lines, boundaries and illustrations. Chinese and Western artwork brightness are remembered separately. Changing tradition preserves the time and field.

sections.title: 6.3 Choose labels for the preview and the photograph
sections.html:
• Select star names and Bayer designations, catalog IDs for unnamed stars, or Solar System names. Deep-sky categories include selected objects, the Messier catalog and all listed objects. A catalog symbol marks position; imagery depends on survey coverage.
  • Reduce density for clearer text or zoom to include fainter stars. Maximum density permits overlapping labels. The equatorial grid and ecliptic use the simulated date in both traditions.
  • The main scene, viewfinder and exported optical photograph have separate display switches. Categories, density and sky tradition are shared. Enable “Finder sky annotations” and clear “Include annotations in photos” to see names while framing and save a clean image.

sections.title: 6.4 Visit a star and see a constellation from the side
sections.html:
The key diagram opens on first entry. Click the sky, press H to move forward and Space to stop. Reopen it from Controls. Set the centre-of-view marker to a ring, an open cross, a dot or hidden, with a colour and an outline.

  1. Open “Interstellar travel” under “Orbit & time” or in the world view’s top bar. Search by name, HIP number, constellation or asterism; shortcuts include Sirius, Vega and the Big Dipper.
  2. “Aim at target” turns the camera. “Travel to star” travels to the star. Press Space or choose “Stop” to halt. Set the cruise speed and enable automatic slowdown near a star when needed. Travel also works while the simulation clock is paused.
  3. Click the view. H/N move forward/back, J/L left/right and I/K down/up. W/S tilt, A/D turn and Q/E roll. Drag to change direction and scroll to change field of view.
  4. Expand the sky-chart settings, select the tradition and figure, show 3D lines and choose “View from the side”. A 3D segment requires reliable distances for both endpoints. Use the near-Sun viewpoint to see the figure from home or enable the solar-view reference for the familiar artwork and survey imagery.
  5. “Look back at the Sun” looks back from your location. “Return near the Sun” travels back near Earth’s orbit at the current date. The Solar System and ground comparison buttons open the corresponding worlds.

sections.title: 6.5 Read the navigation map and save a waypoint
sections.html: The lower-right interstellar map initially follows you within 20 light-years. Gold marks the Sun and target, cyan marks your location and sight line, and purple marks motion. Drag the 3D sphere to see depth; scroll or use plus/minus for scale. Top and side views separate overlapping stars. Clicking selects a star; for a cluster choose an item in the list, then look at it or travel to it. In the full map select yourself, the Sun or the target as center. Inspect target distance, height and nearest star. Fit the map to include both yourself and the target, or reset to the default orientation. Toggle names, track and connecting lines separately. Map layout and range are remembered; the current travel track retains up to 512 samples. Name and save a waypoint to store position, orientation, field of view, selected target and chart. Up to 12 waypoints can be kept. Select its diamond and choose the restore command to return. The top photo button exports the sky, active labels, location and time without the navigation panel.

title: The Moon, planetary observations and the cosmic gallery

sections.title: 7.1 Observe the Moon at your chosen site and time
sections.html:
1. Open “Lunar observatory” from the Earth and sky settings or the mission lab. When Xuntian targets the Moon, its lunar card also opens the workstation.
  2. Choose ground observation. Enter latitude, east longitude and altitude in the observation site panel, then apply the site or load the saved observing site. Beijing is the initial example.
  3. This workstation uses UTC. Subtract eight hours from Beijing time. It starts from the main scene time and then runs independently. Apply the entered time, select today, previous/next day or read the main scene time again. Supported dates span 1900–2100.
  4. The lunar disk has celestial north at the top. Scroll to zoom. Read illuminated fraction, distance, apparent diameter and geometric altitude. Negative altitude means the Moon is below your horizon; the theoretical lunar disk is still available. Libration shows changes in the portion we see. Enter the telescope aperture to estimate ideal angular resolution.
  5. Use the rise/set and phase calculation for the next 48 hours of rising, setting and upper transit and the next four major phases. Times use an ideal horizon. Select a phase to go there. A lunation plays back at one day per second and pauses when you leave.

sections.title: 7.2 Find lunar features, landing sites and geological regions
sections.html:
Goal Action
Explore the far side or terrain Select the 3D lunar surface. Drag to rotate and click to read latitude, east longitude and elevation. Use simulated visible light or false-color LOLA elevation. Choose true relief (1×) or exaggerated relief (8×).
Identify a crater or landing site Search the feature and landing-site index by formal name, Chinese alias, mission or rover. Filter by type and select a result for location and details. Place labels, landing markers and density are independent. Chinese missions have red stars; rover markers identify the associated landing site.
Explore the terminator Select an exploration target and fly to it in 3D. Follow the terminator to find a low-Sun site on the visible face, or explore the far side. Try a different date if no suitable target is available.
Read lunar geology Select the Chinese Academy of Sciences geological layer. Rotate the globe to compare units. Open the full 2022 map for its legend and time scale. Colors represent geological classes; gray indicates unavailable source samples.

Save the lunar image as a PNG with site, time, layer, relief scale and active markers. The workstation remembers layers, selected target and label preferences. Reopening the workstation sets its time and camera anew. The Xuntian lunar handoff uses the spacecraft position and main-scene time.

sections.title: 7.3 Explore Mars and observe it from Earth
sections.html: Open “Celestial observatory” (under “Tools” on small screens). The top selector offers Mars, Earth, the Sun and the Moon. The Sun opens Xuntian solar observing and the Moon opens the lunar workstation. For Mars choose 3D exploration, drag and scroll. Search place names or choose a tour site. Compare visible light, daytime or nighttime thermal infrared, elevation and geological layers. Control relief, map lighting, place names and landing sites separately. Click the surface for coordinates, then inspect the layer legend and source. Unobserved polar regions in nighttime infrared use a neutral color. For a telescope view from Earth, enter the terrestrial observing site and altitude, apply it and choose the Earth-based telescope view. The field is measured in arcseconds. Compare Mars’s apparent diameter, distance, illumination and central meridian; azimuth and altitude locate it in your local sky. This observatory uses UTC+8 and supports 1900–2100.

sections.title: 7.4 Read Earth imagery, surface temperature, elevation and mineral sites
sections.html:
Choose Earth in the observatory and change its surface layer. Pick a place or point on the globe and choose “Explore the ground here” to enter ground observation there.

Layer How to read it
Day surface and night lights Use the main scene’s imagery. Simulation time controls lighting; the source panel lists cloud observation time separately.
Visible 1–4–3, near infrared 1–2–1, shortwave infrared 7–2–1 Compare reflectance in the same area. Near infrared helps reveal vegetation; shortwave infrared distinguishes surface types and snow. Check the color key and data date.
Day/night land-surface temperature Degrees Celsius represent clear-sky surface temperature for the map’s data period. Dark hatching marks oceans or missing data.
Land and seafloor elevation Blue indicates ocean floor and green through white indicates land. Click to read overview elevation in metres.

Overlay mineral deposits and occurrences on any map. Choose a commodity, set marker brightness or search the original site name or ID. Zoom into a gold cluster to reveal individual entries; select a record for commodity, position and source, or open the USGS entry. Counts refer to historical records.

sections.title: 7.5 Compare two views, find an event and take a photo
sections.html: Expand the comparison panel. Select different layers and choose the right-hand layer for a side-by-side view, for example Mars geology versus relief, or daytime versus nighttime Earth temperature. Mars also offers two dates with the same field of view. Enter and apply the comparison time. For Earth’s ordinary surface imagery you can compare illumination times. Scientific map layers refer to their own observation periods. For astronomical events choose Mars opposition, solar or lunar eclipses, or Jovian satellite phenomena. Enter your Earth site and start the search. Select a result to open its time and view. The seven-day Jupiter list estimates transits, occultations, eclipses and shadow transits. Choose “Take photo” to export a single- or dual-panel image with labels, layers, time, location and sources; science layers include the data period, scale and selected commodity where applicable.

sections.title: 7.6 Run a demonstration in the cosmic gallery
sections.html:
Open “Universe explorer” from the toolbar or mission lab. Pick a topic, drag to rotate and scroll or pinch to zoom. Drag the progress slider to inspect an instant. Play, pause or restart the demonstration; reset the view to restore the camera.

Topic Try this
Supernova Follow the progenitor, core collapse, ejecta and expanding remnant. Use Xuntian to locate a real remnant such as the Crab Nebula.
Neutron star Change mass or radius and compare mean density and compactness.
Pulsar Change the spin period, magnetic inclination and observer angle to see when a pulse arrives. Gold marks the measurement observer; rotating the camera changes the watching angle.
Meteor Change entry speed and angle above the horizontal to examine the luminous path and elapsed time. A link opens the main scene’s meteor effect.
Black hole Change mass and disk viewing angle to examine the horizon scale and disk appearance. Xuntian points to actual host galaxies including M87 and NGC 5128.

Each cycle uses a separate 20-second teaching timeline. Save the illustration with its parameters and progress. This browser remembers the topic, parameters and progress. Closing or switching experiments stops playback. A Xuntian handoff selects the station mission and aims using the main scene time.

title: Plan a sighting or a photographic observation

sections.title: 8.1 Find a spacecraft pass above your home
sections.html:
1. Select the spacecraft in the main window. Open “Mission lab” → “Pass predictions” (under “Tools” on narrow screens). The main simulation pauses while the lab is open. Try Beijing or enter the site name, latitude, longitude and altitude in metres. North and east coordinates are positive.
  2. Use the simulation time or the current time. Set a 24-, 48-, 72-hour or one-week interval and choose the minimum elevation (5° by default; 0° for the geometric horizon). Press “Predict passes”. Pass, balcony and scheduling times are displayed in UTC+8.
  3. Choose a pass to read the time it crosses your elevation threshold, reaches maximum elevation and descends below the threshold. Read time along the graph and elevation vertically. Drag the slider to read azimuth and elevation. North is 0°, east 90°, south 180° and west 270°. Elevation runs from 0° at the horizon to 90° overhead.
  4. The cyan interval is a candidate sighting: the sky must be dark enough and the spacecraft sunlit. Choose “Show peak in orbit overview” to inspect the highest point on the orbit or “View from the balcony” to include your skyline. Export a selected pass as an ICS calendar event. The header identifies the vehicle, orbit record span and computation mode. Use the latest local ephemeris when available. Ordinary predictions continue beyond the original interval with a propagated orbit, so later maneuvers can change the actual pass. Historical playback uses the original record and returns to its start if the chosen time lies outside it. Early Dongfanghong 1 scenes use a reconstructed orbit.

sections.title: 8.2 Find previous, next and multiple high passes
sections.html:
Pass predictions and balcony observing have independent query panels. Expand high-elevation passes, set the minimum peak elevation (default 60°, range 0–90°) and choose day, night or both.

Query Action
Closest match before or after a time Select previous or next. The search can extend past the ordinary one-week forecast. Stop a long search with the stop button. Entry and exit for these matches use the horizon.
All matches until a date In the filtered list enter the end time or choose the next 30 days, next 90 days or the end of the year. Generate the list. It includes the start and excludes the end. Select a peak time for details. Generate it again after changing conditions.
Candidate visual sightings Enable the visual filter to require a sunlit spacecraft and the local Sun below −6° at the peak. The ordinary day/night filter is based on the local Sun’s altitude at the peak. Balcony results also show the available window after obstructions. Check cloud cover and actual sky brightness separately.

sections.title: 8.3 Preview or watch a pass from your balcony
sections.html:
1. In “Balcony observing” choose Tiangong, Dongfanghong 1 or an imported Earth-orbiting target. Select the Beijing example or enter and save your site, coordinates and altitude. Using device location prompts for permission; check the resulting altitude.
  2. Edit your roof and treetop outline. Set azimuth and obstruction elevation and add or update a vertex, or draw points by clicking the sky. Delete a vertex to correct one point; select a flat horizon to clear the outline. Set site altitude and the skyline separately.
  3. Calculate passes, select a result and open its observing window. Inspect darkness, spacecraft illumination and obstruction. Temporarily disable building and tree obstructions to compare your balcony and an open field; turn them back on to reuse the outline.
  4. In preview mode drag time or replay at 1×, 10× or 30×. The live-watch mode follows system time for a window that has not ended. A pass result can open the same window in balcony preview or watch mode. A Tiangong pass can also be used in the orbital long-exposure experiment. The hemisphere opens looking at the zenith with north up. The horizon preset faces southwest. The full sphere includes the nadir and can show the sky below the horizon; the flat view is useful for reading angles. Drag to look around and scroll or pinch to zoom. On supported devices enable orientation tracking, point toward known north and calibrate it. Recalibrate if the heading drifts, or drag manually.

sections.title: 8.4 Make a long exposure from a station camera
sections.html:
1. Choose “Orbital long exposure”. Select a recommended night pass or the main scene time. A station-fixed camera produces star trails. A star-locked camera shows Earth and station movement over the same exposure. For ground-point lock enter a site and search for a suitable pass.
  2. Select an array and horizon view, a close view of Tianhe, a wide station view or a view into the star field. Check the live framing at the start of the exposure. The detailed controls change the camera position, direction, roll and field. Toggle photographic fill light for a night-side camera.
  3. Enable free framing and click inside the frame. Drag or steer with W/S, A/D and Q/E. H/N moves forward/back, J/L left/right and I/K down/up. Esc or a click outside releases the keys. Reset the current camera preset to recover its original framing.
  4. Choose a preset exposure from one second to ten minutes and generate a preview. In comparison mode drag the divider across the two images of the same interval. Choose the split view or either image, then download a 1080p PNG.

sections.title: 8.5 Schedule a four-tile Xuntian mosaic for one orbit
sections.html:
1. Search a name, catalogue ID (for example M57) or J2000 RA/Dec, or use the current finder centre. Check the field and imagery, then take a single PNG, open the finder, or automatically schedule all four tiles and run the orbit. Manual scheduling retains tile, timing and exposure controls.
  2. Open the orbit and schedule view. Select a row or tile to see valid imaging intervals, Earth occultation and Sun avoidance on the orbit. Click an interval or drag the timeline to compare orbit-relative and UTC+8 times. Use the automatic four-tile arrangement to resolve conflicts. If this field cannot be completed in one orbit, choose a suggested field or enable fewer tiles.
  3. Choose the sky layer and run one orbit, or jump to the end of the last exposure. With at least one completed tile, view the image or download the mosaic PNG. Hatching marks unfinished tiles; the image includes the field, tile labels and total exposure.
  4. To take a live optical image instead, choose the retake button for a tile, aim at that tile, capture it and view the four-tile results. Repeat as needed and export the in-orbit four-tile PNG. The simulated exposure mosaic and the live optical mosaic have separate outputs. Live photos are also kept in the observation journal.

sections.title: 8.6 Save observations and recover original images
sections.html: In the balcony, orbital long-exposure or survey experiment choose “Save this observation”. Open “Observation log”, filter by type and reopen an entry to restore its experiment and parameters. Entries with original photographs also offer image viewing and downloading. Deletion requires confirmation. Records belong to this browser. Download PNG for an independent picture or export ICS in the pass predictor for a calendar reminder.

sections.title: 9.1 Choose daylight, night and terrain layers
sections.html:
Setting What it controls
“Earth & stars” → “Quality” The 1K, 2K, 4K and 8K tiers set the base Earth map and available effects. The fine tier is the default. Medium and above add details for the current view; the simple tier turns off the night layer. Read the loading status below the selector. On iPhone and iPad, Fine uses a 4K globe and a 4K Milky Way. Zoom in for local terrain detail.
Day surface The default is the 2026 Q2 500 m map. The same quarter is available at 1 km, or you can use the original 2004 NASA map. The 2026 product combines April–June land observations and fills ocean and missing areas with a continuous base.
Night lights Choose 2025 at 500 m (default), 2024 at 1 km or the original 2016 data at 1 km. Compare at the same site and time. At ground level neighboring city blocks may merge into bright patches; choose “High altitude” for the city pattern. Day and night map years are selected independently.
True terrain, height 1× Tilt the view to inspect relief. A global base is bundled and local elevation loads as needed. Use the retry control under terrain data and cache if loading fails. See city imagery.

sections.title: 9.2 Control clouds, cloud maps and auroras
sections.html:
Open the cloud library under “Earth & stars” → “Clouds & aurora”. Preview a saved map and read its source and date. “Use this map” applies it; the current indicator marks the loaded version. You can switch back to the built-in static map, procedural generation or no clouds. Downloading a new map leaves the displayed map in place. See data updates.

Cloud source Coverage and interpretation
Live Cloud Maps Global visual composite with static high-latitude fill.
NOAA GMGSI Recently published hourly infrared mosaic, with cold clouds prominent and static polar fill.
NASA SatCORPS Choose a month, date and observation time. The library distinguishes global, regional and unverified coverage.
Himawari-9 Asia-Pacific cloud classification at roughly ten-minute intervals. The surface is visible outside coverage or in observation gaps.
Canadian GDPS A forecast of total cloud cover including both poles. Check both the forecast initialization and valid times.

The cloud layer switch controls visibility, and cloud opacity under sky and exposure controls its appearance. Night-side clouds obscure city lights; turn that option off to inspect the light map directly. Volumetric and dynamic clouds are available in 8K. Changing simulation time changes lighting and animation; cloud observation or forecast times are listed separately. Select procedural, latest downloaded or historical aurora data and adjust brightness. For historical data choose an aurora snapshot. The 4K tier uses a classic aurora; 8K draws layered curtains. Pausing freezes the shape. NOAA OVATION data supply activity and extent; the model supplies the fine structure. Change the seed to vary procedural details.

Auroras are enabled by default and generated locally, including offline.

sections.title: 9.3 Set geographic names, sky brightness and atmospheric effects
sections.html: Under “Geography & star chart” → “Earth place labels” enable geographic labels. Select countries, capitals, major cities, borders, seas, mountains, rivers and lakes. The city tier and density determine how many names appear. The overhead label shows the region beneath the spacecraft; Beijing is marked by a red star. Under “Earth & stars” → “Sky & exposure” choose a 4K star-field view, enhanced 16K Milky Way or subdued photographic sky. Toggle the Milky Way and adjust sky brightness or fixed exposure. Choose DSS, Pan-STARRS, Hubble or Webb from the sky imagery selector. See sky imagery. Under “Display & views” enable fill light to inspect a dark hull, or show the Sun direction. In the orbit overview combine the space trajectory and ground track to see how the path projects onto Earth. In the weather and phenomena panel choose the natural or enhanced style. In-cloud lightning, upper-atmosphere flashes, night airglow and meteors can each be switched on or off.

sections.title: 9.4 Improve responsiveness
sections.html: If rotation is slow, turn off volumetric clouds first. If needed, lower the Earth tier from 8K to 4K or try the 4K star-field setting for the sky. Keep automatic performance optimization enabled to adapt atmospheric and volumetric sampling. Orbit calculations and the selected quality tier remain consistent. After zooming, pause the camera briefly and check the actual source and loaded resolution in the surface, sky or terrain status.

sections.title: 10.1 Choose the right way to save
sections.html:
What to keep Control Result
Main scene picture “Photography & scenes” → “Save screenshot” or “Save 4K image” A PNG at the current size, or up to 3840 pixels wide at the current aspect ratio, subject to device limits.
Optical image “Xuntian viewfinder” → “Capture PNG” An image with the viewfinder composition, output size and photo label settings. See Chapter 4.
Favorite environment, time and camera Name and save an environment and camera preset. Choose it later and restore the preset. The station assembly and download policy stay in place.
A scene you can reopen or share “Photography & scenes” → “Scene sharing” → “Export scene” A .starorbit.json file with mission, assembly, array angles, orientation, time, cameras, environment and orbit.

Photo mode hides the interface and minimap. Use the exit button or Esc to return. Clear the spacecraft name switch for a clean hull. Fixed exposure helps match the brightness of successive images.

sections.title: 10.2 Send a scene to another player
sections.html:
1. Enter a scene name and choose “Export scene”. Export ends the main-navball near-orbit exercise and saves the reference orbit. Include the original custom spacecraft model or mission package if needed.
  2. Export the selected downloaded cloud or aurora snapshot if you want the same weather. The scene refers to those records, and the snapshots contain the image data. Music and free-flight saves use their own storage.
  3. On the receiving device install the mission and import the weather snapshots first. Choose “Import scene” and select the scene file. It opens paused at the saved time. Resume when ready. A scene file can be up to 16 MB.
  4. A missing cloud snapshot falls back to the built-in map and a missing aurora snapshot switches auroras off. Import the needed snapshot, then import the scene again.

sections.title: 10.3 Make a birthday sky card
sections.html:
1. Open “Photography & scenes” → “Birthday sky card” and enter a Gregorian birthday from 1901 to 2100. Add optional recipient, sender and presentation date.
  2. On the greeting side choose Western, Chinese or paired panels. Select the birthday card layout or a plain sky map. Adjust artwork, lines and descriptions; select another greeting or edit the text yourself.
  3. Switch to the sky side and choose the Eastern or Western birthday field. Select a Milky Way or DSS optical background. DSS needs a connection on the first visit. Names, connecting lines, artwork, planets, deep-sky objects, grid and ecliptic have independent switches. Open framing to pan, zoom or roll; return to the target to reset the composition.
  4. Set the back to landscape 2400×1500, portrait 1800×2400 or the same size as the front. Generate a preview after changes. Export the current face as PNG or save both images in one ZIP. Western zodiac signs use the Sun’s position in the tropical zodiac. Near a boundary, expand the date explanation and supply birth time and UTC offset, or start with a Chinese card. The Chinese mansion of the day uses the Gregorian date’s earthly branch and weekday, changing at midnight. The reverse-side Sun, Moon and planets use the birthday time, or 20:00 if omitted (UTC+8 by default). Viewing the field in Xuntian uses the main scene time and requires the station mission.

sections.title: 10.4 Play music and edit the playlist
sections.html:
Hover over the music note in the lower-left corner, or tap it on a touchscreen. Play, pause, skip tracks or drag the progress slider. The volume control also offers mute. Open the playlist with the track name or list icon.

  • Add multiple files using “Add music”. Supported formats include M4A, MP3, WAV, OGG, AAC, FLAC and WebM. The limit is 100 MB per file; matching content reuses the existing copy.
  • Select a track to play it. Drag entries or use the up/down controls to reorder. Removing a library entry leaves the original file on your computer. Restore the built-in music to bring back bundled tracks.
  • The startup setting enables playback with a random first track. If the browser waits for a gesture, press Play. Simulation speed and music playback speed are independent.

sections.title: 10.5 Listen to Dongfanghong 1 and read the telemetry
sections.html:
Switch to Dongfanghong 1 and open the signal panel in the player. The historical recording repeats after a five-second gap. Simulated live telemetry derives the instrument signal from the simulated orbit, attitude and spin.

Channel What to inspect
Continuous Sun sensor Compare the solar probe voltage and the yellow trace as attitude changes.
Continuous infrared horizon sensor Compare the Earth direction and the cyan trace.
Ten-second experiment sequence The sequence cycles through reference levels, solar and infrared channels. Compare the selected voltage and subcarrier frequency with the sound.

Telemetry requires a valid orbit and 1× time progression. After pausing, accelerating or jumping in time, return to the foreground and choose the command to run at 1× and listen. Rotating the observation camera does not rotate the sensor. The ordinary playlist resumes its previous position and state when you leave this mission.

sections.title: 11.1 Check sources and choose an update
sections.html:
Open “Data & resources” in the toolbar. Each resource card identifies the source, date, active version and available updates. Observation time, download time and simulation time can differ.

Resource Where to look How to use it
Current spacecraft orbit Check for an orbit update or import orbit data. The station uses official OEM records and modern Dongfanghong 1 uses CelesTrak. For a custom vehicle choose its matching source or file.
Clouds Open the cloud library. Choose source and time, download the map, then select the saved record and apply it.
Auroras Check for an aurora update or import a snapshot. NOAA activity describes the extent and intensity. A historical snapshot stays selected when you check for new data.
Sun Open the solar observation card. Select the band before updating or importing a snapshot. Read the independent UTC observation time. See solar observing.
Surface, cities, sky and elevation Use the relevant surface, night, city or sky resource panel. Global base maps ship with the version, complete city packages can be saved, and local terrain and sky fields load as needed. Inspect their individual caches.

The check-all command handles the cloud catalog, aurora and orbit. Solar updates are per band. In the update log, identify the failed source before retrying; loaded data can still be used.

Save an image or field in the gallery, or save the current field in Xuntian. Manage saved fields and downloads under High-resolution sky data. Clearing the browsing cache keeps your saved imagery.

sections.title: 11.2 Import an orbit for the selected spacecraft
sections.html:
Choose a file under “Orbit & time” → “Orbit data” or use the orbit card in “Data & resources”.

File Requirements
OEM ephemeris One segment centered on EARTH, EME2000 frame and UTC. Position in km, velocity in km/s.
Position and velocity JSON StarOrbit orbit JSON with dated position and velocity samples.
CelesTrak GP/OMM JSON Public orbital elements for the selected spacecraft, using TEME, UTC and SGP4.

Confirm the current mission before importing. The application checks known spacecraft IDs; verify the source of generic ephemerides yourself. Inspect the reported epoch and original coverage. Outside the recorded span, read the displayed extrapolation or historical mode. Use the newest suitable orbit for distant observation dates. See Chapter 2.

sections.title: 11.3 Download, pin or transfer a cloud map
sections.html:
1. Open the cloud library from the resources window or the Earth cloud settings. In the download tab choose a source and the latest frame or a published historical time.
  2. The web viewer can download Live Cloud Maps and Canadian GDPS directly and import converted snapshots. The local service also processes NOAA GMGSI, NASA SatCORPS and Himawari-9. Direct downloads run in the current page; server jobs can be checked again after reopening it.
  3. In saved maps, check the preview, time and coverage before applying the map. Favorite a version to keep it; export its snapshot and import it on the other device to transfer it. Return to the built-in static map when desired.
  4. In the NASA download catalog, the 95% global-coverage filter requires estimated global coverage of at least 95% and at least 85% in each polar region. The saved NASA global group uses stricter checks on complete products. Use the full list for regional or unverified records. See cloud sources.

sections.title: 11.4 Check what a cache cleanup will remove
sections.html:
Storage What happens
Downloaded weather and orbits Inspect usage, history and favorites in the download cache panel. Automatic limits are on by default, with an initial 200 MB limit adjustable from 20 to 2000 MB. Cleanup begins with eligible older records and protects active, favorite and referenced records.
Saved clouds Deleting a map requires confirmation and may delete the corresponding local library file and browser copy. The active map switches to the built-in map before deletion. Complete or cancel downloads first. When clearing the cloud cache in bulk, local files are also removed; retaining favorites protects the browser’s favorite copies.
Local cloud library The launcher restores suitable files under ~/Library/Application Support/Tiangong Orbit Simulator/clouds. Matching local and browser copies from the same observation are merged in the list. Automatic browser limits apply to the browser copy.
Cities, elevation and sky surveys Clearing roaming imagery keeps complete offline city packages. Elevation and sky imagery have separate caches. Automatically downloaded tiles cover the fields already visited. See terrain and sky surveys.

sections.title: 11.5 Reopen a task, move devices or restore settings
sections.html:
Item Saving and restoring
Routine settings The same browser and address restore ordinary mission, assembly, environment and interface preferences. Real-time mode returns to the present; custom time resumes at the saved instant. A different hostname, port or directly opened file has separate storage.
Scene and camera presets Transfer a scene file across devices. Restore a favorite view from its original list. Keep custom models, music and weather snapshots separately. See scene sharing.
Free flight, docking and observations Save a free-flight mission or return to observation to continue it later. Docking exports JSON/CSV reports. Use the observation journal to reopen observing experiments. See flight and the journal.
Main-navball exercise This controls the present session. Returning to observation, changing missions or jumping in time ends the exercise. Use free flight for a persistent flying mission.
Window layout, assembly or all preferences Restore the window layout in display settings. Restoring the default assembly also resets relevant angles and camera. Factory reset under display settings resets preferences and assembly after confirmation and preserves downloads and favorites.

sections.title: 11.6 Troubleshoot by symptom
sections.html:
What you see Try this
Interface visible but spacecraft and surroundings dark Go to a gold sunlit segment on the event timeline, or enable fill light for the hull. Nighttime oceans have little surface lighting.
City lights form a bright patch close to the ground The default night map has about 500 m resolution. Go to high altitude for the pattern across the city.
City found in the telescope but no surface visible Check that the city is on the visible side and has daylight. Try the Beijing and Vega example.
Switching to DSS makes little visible difference Zoom in and inspect the source and band. Uncached DSS and Pan-STARRS fields need connectivity, and selected Webb images cover specific fields.
Names in the viewfinder do not appear on the photo Enable “Include annotations in photos”. Verify the name categories and density, then take a new photograph.
A predicted pass is hidden from the balcony Inspect sunlight, local twilight and direction in the pass record. Compare them with your skyline and the actual weather. See Chapter 8.
Scene or playlist missing after changing browsers Return to the original browser and address, or transfer the scene, weather snapshots and original media files.
Slow graphics, interrupted updates or silent telemetry Try a lower Earth tier or turn off volumetric clouds. Read the update log and use a saved record. For telemetry, return to the foreground and run the simulation at 1×.
